standard.sentence: ___ comida de México es muy famosa.
standard.english: Food from Mexico is very famous.
standard.rewritten: La comida de México es muy famosa.
standard.explanation: Generic or general references to nouns require a definite article in Spanish, unlike in English. Because 'comida' is feminine singular, 'la' is used.
Abstract nouns like 'amor' require a definite article in Spanish. 'Amor' is masculine singular, so 'el' is used.
Classifying 'ser' sentences without extra adjectives can omit the article.

standard.sentence: Lo que escribió es ___ mentira más horrible que he leído.
standard.english: What he wrote is the worst lie I have ever read.
standard.rewritten: Lo que escribió es la mentira más horrible que he leído.
standard.explanation: Superlative constructions use the definite article.

standard.sentence: Lo que dijo es ___ pura verdad.
standard.english: What he said is the absolute truth.
standard.rewritten: Lo que dijo es la pura verdad.
standard.explanation: While 'es verdad' on its own can omit the definite article, adding a modifying adjective like 'pura' specifies the noun and requires the definite article 'la'.

standard.sentence: Me lavo ___ manos antes de comer.
standard.english: I wash my hands before eating.
standard.rewritten: Me lavo las manos antes de comer.
standard.explanation: Body parts used with reflexive verbs use definite articles ('las') instead of possessive adjectives ('my').

standard.sentence: Siempre tengo una reunión en la mañana ___ lunes.
standard.english: I always have a meeting in the morning on Mondays.
standard.rewritten: Siempre tengo una reunión en la mañana los lunes.
standard.explanation: When referring to recurring days of the week, Spanish uses the plural definite article ('los') instead of a preposition like 'on'.

standard.sentence: No puedo creerlo. Ya es ___ viernes.
standard.english: I can't believe it. It's already Friday.
standard.rewritten: No puedo creerlo. Ya es viernes.
standard.explanation: Days of the week stated with ser do not require a definite article.
Omit the definite article when languages is used directly as an object of verbs like 'hablar', 'estudiar', or 'aprender'.

standard.sentence: ___ maestra Martínez llegó a la aula.
standard.english: Professor Martínez arrived to the classroom.
standard.rewritten: La maestra Martínez llegó a la aula.
standard.explanation: Professional titles require a definite article when talking about someone in the third person.
When addressing someone directly using their title, the definite article is omitted.

standard.rewritten: Julio es el alcalde del pueblo.
standard.explanation: Identifying sentences with ser, when you say someone is a specific person or something is a specific thing use the definite article.

standard.sentence: Carlos es ___ traductor mexicano que trabaja aquí.
standard.english: Carlos is the Mexican translator who works here.
standard.rewritten: Carlos es el traductor mexicano que trabaja aquí.
standard.explanation: Normally classifying professions omit articles ('Carlos es traductor'), but using it together with an adjective ('mexicano') and adding a descriptive clause ('que trabaja aquí') specifies the person and the phrase therefore requires 'el'.

all.rewritten: Le ingeniere Martínez diseñó el puente.
all.explanation: Titles when talking about a non-binary individual require the non-binary singular definite article 'le'.

all.sentence: ___ amigues de Álex vienen a la fiesta.
all.english: Álex's friends are coming to the party.
all.rewritten: Les amigues de Álex vienen a la fiesta.
all.explanation: When referring to a plural group of non-binary or gender non-conforming individuals in the third person, the non-binary plural article 'les' is used.
When referring to a non-binary or gender non-conforming individual in the third person, the non-binary plural article 'le' is used.
Direct address omits the article, regardless of whether standard or inclusive terminology is used.
